overview: This file documents the political and industrial backlash against a 1946 proposal to recruit two American ceramic engineers to advise the military government in occupied Japan. Pottery manufacturers, trade organizations, municipal officials, and members of Congress argued that taxpayer-funded technical assistance would rebuild Japan’s low-cost ceramics industry, threaten American factories and jobs, and revive allegedly unfair competition. Some critics proposed imposing American-style wages, hours, welfare provisions, and social-security standards on Japanese industry instead. The State Department repeatedly clarified that the War Department would have employed and paid the advisers, but the controversy effectively ended when General Douglas MacArthur withdrew the request.
interest: The file offers a compact case study of the conflict between American plans for Japan’s economic rehabilitation and domestic fears of renewed foreign competition. Its unusually concentrated body of protests reveals how manufacturers and workers mobilized mayors, chambers of commerce, senators, and representatives to influence occupation policy. It is especially useful for historians studying postwar trade politics, deindustrialization anxieties, congressional pressure on the executive branch, and attempts to make labor and welfare standards part of the international economic order.
